scenes.heading: Pointers
scenes.narration: Let's demystify Pointers, the values that hold a memory address instead of the data itself.

scenes.heading: The whole mechanic
items: A pointer holds the address of a value
Use * to read or write through it
The zero value of a pointer is nil
scenes.narration: A pointer is simply the address of a value in memory, and its type is star T. There are only two operators to learn. The ampersand takes the address of a value, giving you a pointer. The star dereferences that pointer to read or write the value it points at. And every pointer's zero value is nil, meaning it points at nothing.

scenes.heading: How inc(&n) mutates the caller
steps: n lives at some address in main
Back in main, n has changed
scenes.narration: Go passes arguments by value, so how does a function change its caller's variable? Say n lives at some address in main. Ampersand n produces that address. When you call inc, the function receives a copy of the pointer, but that copy still holds the same address. Inside, star p plus plus follows the address and increments the value there. Back in main, n reflects the change, because the function wrote to n's actual memory.

scenes.heading: Pass by pointer to mutate
scenes.narration: Here it is in code. The inc function takes a star int, and star p plus plus dereferences the pointer and increments what it points to. In main we call inc with ampersand n twice, passing n's address each time. Because both calls write through to the real n, the final value is three. Without the pointer, inc would only ever bump a throwaway copy.

scenes.text: Dereferencing a nil pointer panics — check for nil before *p, and remember Go has no pointer arithmetic.
scenes.narration: One rule keeps pointers safe: dereferencing a nil pointer panics at runtime, so check for nil before you follow a pointer that might be unset. The good news is that Go has no pointer arithmetic and a garbage collector tracks memory, so you can't fabricate addresses or leak memory the way you can in C.
